bullets: How a population grows almost exponentially at first, then bends over and levels exactly at the carrying capacity K
slides.heading: Logistic growth: bending to the carrying capacity
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we follow one population curve as it bends - steep at first, then flattening to its ceiling.

bullets: Describe logistic growth: the curve bends over and levels at the carrying capacity K
Explain why every starting population is funnelled to the same equilibrium, and how harvesting drags that equilibrium down
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud and tell the class: by the end you will be able to explain why the curve bends and where it settles.

bullets: A small population doubles quickly, then doubles again
So does it keep doubling for ever, level off, or crash back down?
slides.heading: Fast growth - for ever?
slides.notes: Ask the class: the population is growing faster and faster - what happens next? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the ceiling decides.

bullets: The environment can support at most K individuals; K is the carrying capacity
As P nears K the growth rate falls towards zero, so the curve bends over instead of steepening for ever
At P = K the growth rate is exactly zero: K is a stable equilibrium
slides.heading: The carrying capacity caps growth
slides.notes: Stress the deciding idea: never extrapolate the early steep rise - check how close P is to K first, because the factor (1 - P/K) is doing the braking.

bullets: The curve rises steeply at first, almost exponentially
Then it bends over and levels exactly at P = K
slides.heading: The logistic curve bends to the ceiling
slides.notes: Play scene 1 and point to the dashed ceiling: follow the marker along the curve as it bends towards P = K.

bullets: Slope ticks are steep for small populations and flatten near K
Low, middle and high starting curves all settle at the same K
slides.heading: A slope field funnels all starts to K
slides.notes: Play scene 2 and watch the three starts: name where the ticks are steep and where they flatten before the curves settle.

bullets: dP/dt = rP(1 - P/K): the factor (1 - P/K) brakes the growth
The growth rate peaks halfway to K, then falls to zero at P = K
slides.heading: The equation behind the bend
slides.notes: Play scene 3 slowly: follow the rate marker as it climbs, peaks halfway, then dies away to zero at K.

bullets: Steady harvesting removes population every season
The equilibrium drops to a lower level and the population re-settles there
slides.heading: Harvesting drags the equilibrium down
slides.notes: Play scene 4 and follow the equilibrium line: watch it slide down and the settled tail drop with it.

bullets: At small P the factor (1 - P/K) is near 1, so growth is almost exponential with rate rP
Halfway to K the growth rate is at its peak; at P = K it is zero, so the population stops changing
slides.heading: Worked example: reading the bend
slides.notes: Work it slowly: Step 1, evaluate (1 - P/K) at small P - near 1, barely any braking. Step 2, at P = K/2 the rate peaks. Step 3, at P = K the factor is zero and the curve levels.

bullets: In pairs: a population starts above K - sketch its curve and say where it settles, and why
Then swap and check: did your curve bend towards K instead of climbing away?
slides.heading: Your turn: predict the settle point
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes. Listen for ceiling-first reasoning, then take two pairs answers: the curve falls back and settles at P = K, because above K the growth rate is negative.

bullets: Your exit ticket asks you to correct a student who thinks the population keeps accelerating like a pure exponential
Name the falling growth rate and the levelling at P = K to earn full credit
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Point to the exit ticket and remind the class: the strongest answers brake the growth as P nears K instead of extrapolating the early rise.
